title: Containers and Kubernetes
oneLiner: What a container image really is, and how Kubernetes keeps your app running when things break.
keyTakeaway: A container is an ordinary Linux process with its own view of the filesystem and network, started from an image built in cached layers. Kubernetes doesn't run commands for you: you declare what you want (3 copies of version 2), and its controllers keep changing reality until it matches.
explanation:
A container isn't a small virtual machine (a whole simulated computer running its own operating system). It's a normal process on a Linux machine, the same kind you met in the processes lesson, that the kernel (the core of the operating system, shared by every container on the machine) fences off: it sees its own filesystem, its own process list and its own network, and it can be limited to a share of CPU and memory. That's why containers start in milliseconds and why so much of this section is Linux underneath.

The filesystem a container starts with comes from an image, built from a Dockerfile. Each instruction produces a layer, and Docker caches layers: on the next build it reuses everything up to the first instruction whose inputs changed, then re-runs the rest. That's why Dockerfiles copy the project file and restore packages before copying the source code -- try the buttons in part 1 to see the difference it makes. The image is the same artifact on your laptop, in CI and in production, which is most of the point.

Kubernetes runs containers across a group of machines (nodes). You don't tell it to start a container on node 2; you give it a Deployment that says "I want 3 replicas of academy:v1", and a controller loop compares that with what's actually running, over and over, fixing any difference. Each running copy is a pod. Crash a pod or fail a node in part 2 and watch the loop replace what was lost; raise the replicas and it adds more. A Service gives the pods one stable address and spreads requests across the ones that are ready.

Changing the version starts a rolling update: start one new pod, wait until it's ready, retire one old pod, repeat. Users keep being served throughout, which is why apps need to start up and shut down cleanly (remember SIGTERM). A small web app like this one typically needs four objects: a Deployment, a Service, an Ingress and a network policy.

The demo is a simplified model, not a real cluster; the real controllers work the same way, with more detail (health checks, resource requests, scheduling rules).
